column1: What are the three parts of a game?
column2: Players (who decides), strategies (the choices), and payoffs (a number for each player for each combination of choices).

column1: In a payoff grid cell \( (a, b) \), whose payoff is which?
column2: \( a \) goes to the row player, \( b \) to the column player.
A strategy that beats every other strategy of yours no matter what the other players do.
A set of choices where every player plays a best response to the others. Nobody gains by switching alone.

column1: How do you find pure Nash equilibria in a 2x2 grid by hand?
column2: Draw best-response arrows: down each column for the row player, across each row for the column player. A cell no arrow leaves is an equilibrium.

column1: What makes a game a prisoner's dilemma?
column2: \( T > R > P > S \): defecting is dominant, yet mutual defection pays both less than mutual cooperation.

column1: How do you find a 2x2 mixed equilibrium?
column2: Choose your probabilities to make the other player indifferent between their two moves: set their two expected payoffs equal and solve.

column1: What does the Nash existence theorem (1950) guarantee?
column2: Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.
In a finite two-player zero-sum game, \( \max_p \min_q p^T M q = \min_q \max_p p^T M q = v \), the value of the game.
Cooperate in round 1, then copy the last move of the opponent. Nice, retaliating, forgiving and clear.
Adding a free road to a network can make every selfish driver slower at equilibrium (65 to 80 minutes in the classic example).

column1: What is the price of anarchy?
column2: Total cost at the worst equilibrium divided by the best possible total cost. At most \( 4/3 \) for linear delays.

column1: Why bid your true value in a second-price auction?
column2: Your bid only decides whether you win. The price is the second bid. Truthful bidding wins exactly when winning is profitable.
With independent private values, first-price and second-price auctions earn the same expected revenue: \( 100(n-1)/(n+1) \) for values uniform on 0 to 100.

column1: How do you win at Nim?
column2: XOR the heap sizes (the nim-sum). If it is not 0, shrink a heap \( h \) to \( h \oplus s \) to leave a nim-sum of 0. A nim-sum of 0 loses for the player to move.
